igcse-0580-diff-tangent-estimates.description: Draw a tangent at a specified point, choose two points on that line and use the signed rise and run.

sections.title: How do I place a ruler to draw the tangent?
sections.label: Follow the curve

blocks.html: The tangent is a straight line through the point that matches the local direction of the curve. Look just to the left and right of the point when lining up the ruler.

figure.alt: Cartesian graph of a curve through P at (3,0). A straight tangent through P includes A at (1,-4) and B at (5,4). A right-angled triangle shows the rise and run.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Mark the point first. Follow the curve for a short distance near it and adjust the ruler until the line has the same direction there. Draw that line long enough to read two separated points.

blocks.title: Use two points on the same tangent
blocks.prompt: Two measured points on a tangent at \(P\) are \(A(2,7)\) and \(B(6,-5)\). Calculate the gradient of the marked tangent.
blocks.hint: Subtract the two y-values in the same order as the two x-values.
blocks.solution:
Go from A to B. The signed change in height is \(-12\) and the change in x is \(4\).

Divide the change in height by the change in x. The gradient is \(-3\).

retry.feedback: The line slopes down as x increases, so use a negative gradient.
Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.
Divide this vertical change by the horizontal change.

blocks.html: Joining two distant points on the curve gives a secant and measures the change across an interval.

blocks.title: Read the signed rise and run
blocks.prompt: A pupil moves 4 units right along a tangent. The line goes up 14 units. Find the gradient of the tangent exactly.
blocks.hint: Read the line from left to right. A downward change in y is negative.
blocks.solution:
The run is \(4\). The vertical change is \(14\) because the line goes up.

Divide vertical change by horizontal change to get \(\frac{7}{2}\).

retry.feedback: Use rise over run, not the inverse.
Check the sign of the vertical change as you move right.

sections.title: Which two points should I use?
sections.label: Read rise and run

blocks.html: Use points on the line you drew. Pick easy-to-read points well apart, preferably at grid intersections. A shallow line might need quite a long run.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Find \(\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\). Keep the order of subtraction the same above and below the fraction bar. Count actual axis units rather than squares when the scales differ.

blocks.title: Measure a longer segment of a tangent
blocks.prompt: For a drawn tangent at \(x=-1\), a point on the line is \((-4,\frac{15}{2})\). Moving along the line to \(x=2\) gives a vertical change of \(-21\). What gradient does this estimate?
blocks.hint: The horizontal change uses both x-coordinates of the measurement.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal change is \(2-(-4)=6\).

Divide the signed vertical change \(-21\) by the horizontal change. This gives \(-\frac{7}{2}\).

retry.feedback: Use the difference between the two x-coordinates for the run.

blocks.html: A point on the curve that is off the tangent cannot be used for this calculation.

Divide the change in height by the change in x. The gradient is \(\frac{9}{2}\).

retry.feedback: Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.
Divide this vertical change by the horizontal change.

igcse-0580-diff-power-rule.description: Apply the power rule to polynomial terms with rational coefficients, then use the derivative to find a gradient.

sections.title: How do I differentiate one power of x?
sections.label: Multiply and reduce

blocks.html: For \(y=ax^n\) with positive whole-number exponent \(n\), use \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=anx^{n-1}\).

figure.alt: A parabola with negative, zero and positive tangent slopes at x-values minus 2, 0 and 2.
figure.caption: The same curve can have a different gradient at each point.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Multiply the old coefficient by the old exponent. Then reduce the exponent by one. Fractions in the coefficient work in exactly the same way.

Differentiate one term at a time
Term in y\(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\)
\(\frac{3}{4}x^4\)\(3x^3\)
\(-9x\)\(-9\)
\(12\)\(0\)

blocks.title: Find the gradient function
blocks.prompt: Given \(y=-\frac{2}{5}x^6\), find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\). Give the expression for the derivative.
blocks.hint: Multiply by the old power before taking one off that power.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the coefficient of each power by its original exponent. Reduce the exponent by one. A term in x becomes its coefficient.

A constant contributes zero. Combine the remaining terms to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=-\frac{12}{5}x^5\).

retry.feedback: This is the original curve. The gradient function comes from the power rule.
Reducing the exponent is one step. Multiply each coefficient by its original exponent first.

blocks.html: Keep the sign of the original coefficient. Reducing the exponent alone misses the factor from the old exponent.

blocks.title: Find the gradient function
blocks.prompt: Given \(y=2x^4-13x+10\), find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\). Give the expression for the derivative.
blocks.hint: Multiply by the old power before taking one off that power.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the coefficient of each power by its original exponent. Reduce the exponent by one. A term in x becomes its coefficient.

A constant contributes zero. Combine the remaining terms to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=8x^3-13\).

retry.feedback: This is the original curve. The gradient function comes from the power rule.
Reducing the exponent is one step. Multiply each coefficient by its original exponent first.

sections.title: What happens to a term in x or a constant?
sections.label: Differentiate each term

blocks.html: A term \(bx\) has constant gradient \(b\). A constant has zero gradient because its graph is horizontal.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Differentiate each term separately, including its sign, and add the results. For example, \(y=2x^5-7x+3\) gives \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=10x^4-7\).

blocks.title: Differentiate a constant
blocks.prompt: Given \(y=55\), find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\). Give the expression for the derivative.
blocks.hint: Multiply by the old power before taking one off that power.
blocks.solution:
The graph is a horizontal line. Its y-value stays fixed as x changes.

Its gradient is always zero, so \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=0\).

retry.feedback: The y-value is constant. Its change, and therefore the gradient, is zero.

blocks.html: The constant in the original formula does not stay in the derivative. A linear term becomes a constant.

blocks.title: Find the gradient function
blocks.prompt: Given \(y=\frac{4}{3}x^5-11x+6\), find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\). Give the expression for the derivative.
blocks.hint: Multiply by the old power before taking one off that power.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the coefficient of each power by its original exponent. Reduce the exponent by one. A term in x becomes its coefficient.

A constant contributes zero. Combine the remaining terms to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{20}{3}x^4-11\).

retry.feedback: This is the original curve. The gradient function comes from the power rule.
Reducing the exponent is one step. Multiply each coefficient by its original exponent first.

sections.title: How do I get the gradient at a specific x?
sections.label: Evaluate the derivative

blocks.html: The derivative is a rule for gradient. The original formula is a rule for height on the curve. Use the correct formula for the quantity you want.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\) first. Then substitute the x-coordinate. Use brackets around a negative value of x before squaring or cubing it.

blocks.title: Find the exact gradient at a point
blocks.prompt: The curve has equation \(y=4x^3-13x+10\). Find its gradient at \(x=-1\).
blocks.hint: Use the x-value in the gradient function rather than in the equation for y.
blocks.solution:
First differentiate to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=12x^2-13\).

Substitute \(x=-1\) into this derivative. The gradient is \(-1\).

retry.feedback: That is a value of y. The gradient comes from differentiating first.
Include the derivative of the linear term as well.

blocks.html: Putting the x-value into the original expression gives y, not the gradient.

blocks.title: Find a position from a stated gradient
blocks.prompt: At what value of \(x\) does \(y=5x^2+4x+10\) have gradient \(-36\)?
blocks.hint: The gradient value is the result of the derivative, not its input.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=10x+4\).

Set the gradient function equal to \(-36\) and solve. This gives \(x=-4\).

retry.feedback: The question gives that gradient. Solve the derivative equation to find x.

blocks.html: Use \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\) to label the derivative. Keep it separate from the original y equation.

igcse-0580-diff-stationary-coordinates.description: Use a zero derivative to find stationary x-values and the original curve to find each matching y-coordinate.

sections.title: What does a horizontal tangent tell me?
sections.label: Set gradient zero

blocks.html: A horizontal line has gradient zero. At a stationary point, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=0\).

figure.alt: Cubic curve with horizontal tangents at (-1,4) and (1,0).
figure.caption: A zero gradient gives the x-coordinate of a stationary point. Its y-coordinate comes from the curve.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Differentiate first and set the result equal to zero. Solve that equation for x. This gives where the tangent is horizontal.

blocks.title: Find every x-value where the tangent is horizontal
blocks.prompt: At which values of \(x\) is the tangent to \(y=-2x^3+24x+3\) horizontal?
blocks.hint: A horizontal tangent has zero gradient.
blocks.solution:
Horizontal means \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=0\). Solve \(-6x^2+24=0\).

Both \(-2\) and \(2\) satisfy that equation.

retry.feedback: Also include the negative root of the squared equation.

blocks.html: Setting y equal to zero finds where the graph meets the x-axis. The question about a horizontal tangent asks for a zero gradient.

blocks.title: Find both coordinates of a stationary point
blocks.prompt: Find the coordinates of the stationary point on \(y=3x^2+24x\).
blocks.hint: At a stationary point the gradient is zero, but the y-coordinate need not be zero.
blocks.solution:
Solve \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=6x+24=0\). It gives \(x=-4\).

Substitute \(-4\) into the original equation for y to find \(y=-48\).

The resulting coordinates are \((-4,-48)\).

retry.feedback: The derivative is zero here. Find the y-coordinate from the original expression.

sections.title: How do I find both coordinates?
sections.label: Find the height

blocks.html: Use the derivative to find x. Use the curve equation to find y. These two substitutions have different purposes.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: After finding a stationary x-value, put that x into the original equation and write the answer as an ordered pair.

blocks.title: Find both coordinates of a stationary point
blocks.prompt: Find the coordinates of the stationary point on \(y=-7x^2+42x+11\).

What does a horizontal tangent tell me?

A horizontal line has gradient zero. At a stationary point, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=0\).

Differentiate first and set the result equal to zero. Solve that equation for x. This gives where the tangent is horizontal.

How do I find both coordinates?

Use the derivative to find x. Use the curve equation to find y. These two substitutions have different purposes.

After finding a stationary x-value, put that x into the original equation and write the answer as an ordered pair.

What if the derivative has two zeros?

A cubic can yield a polynomial of degree two when differentiated. Its zero-gradient equation can have two different solutions.

blocks.prompt: Find all stationary points of \(y=4x^3-192x-8\). Give both coordinate pairs.
blocks.hint: There are two signs when solving the equation for x squared.
blocks.solution:
Set \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=12x^2-192\) to zero. The equation reduces to \(x^2=16\).

Both \(x=-4\) and \(x=4\) work. Substitute both into the equation for y separately.

The resulting coordinates are \((-4,504),\quad (4,-520)\).

blocks.title: Choose an order for the turning points
blocks.prompt: The equation is \(y=2x^3-24x+4\). The two turning points occur at \(x=-2\) and \(x=2\) from left to right. Which order must the sketch show?
blocks.hint: Follow the curve from left to right through both stationary points.
blocks.solution:
The derivative has one sign between the two roots and the opposite sign outside. The graph goes up, then down, then up.

The turn order is maximum, then minimum.

blocks.title: Find the point where the sketch meets the y-axis
blocks.prompt: For a sketch of \(y=2x^3-24x+11\), find the y-intercept. Give its coordinates.
blocks.hint: Use x = 0 in the original curve equation to find the y-intercept.
blocks.solution:
On the y-axis, \(x=0\). Substitute into the original equation.

Every power of x vanishes. The constant gives \(y=11\).

The resulting coordinates are \((0,11)\).

retry.feedback: The x-coordinate of the y-intercept must be zero.

The second derivative is \(-18x\). It is negative at \(x=3\), so this x gives the local maximum.

Substitute that x into the original equation to get \(y=169\).

revision.body:
Which points should I put on the sketch first?

Mark the axes, plot the stationary points and identify the y-intercept. Their relative positions make it easier to link the branches.

Find the stationary x-values from the derivative and their heights from the original formula. Use \(x=0\) in the original equation for the y-intercept.

Which way should the curve go between the turns?

The derivative tells you where the graph rises or falls. Its sign in each interval fixes the direction of the branch there.

An upward curve that turns down makes a local maximum. The next turn can reverse the direction again. Mark both types before joining the points with a smooth graph.

How can I check the completed sketch?

Read across the sketch in increasing x. Check that the curve has the calculated y-intercept and goes through each stationary point with the expected direction change.
